requirements: The core contributions of NanoFlow (compute-bound analysis of LLM serving, intra-device parallelism via nano-batching, auto-search pipeline construction, runtime with KV-cache offloading, and end-to-end throughput/latency gains over vLLM/DeepSpeed-FastGen/TensorRT-LLM) have been reproduced.

sub_tasks.requirements: The MILP-based Stage-I search over the number/size/ordering of nano-operations (subject to dependency, batch-size discretization, overlap-different-resource, and network-transform constraints) is implemented and produces a feasible pipeline within ~10 minutes.
Inputs and problem-setup plumbing for the Stage-I MILP are present and correct.

Code has been implemented that constructs the Stage-I input from three components: (a) the dense batch size, (b) the operation-level dependency graph parsed from the PyTorch model definition (KQV, attention, O, Up, Gate, Act, Down, plus AG/AR nodes), and (c) the interference-free (kernel, batch_size) -> best_time table produced by kernel profiling.

verification.spec: Import the Stage-I input builder module. Call it with (dense_batch_size=2048, model=LLaMA-2-70B PyTorch definition, kernel_profile_table). Assert the returned object contains (a) a scalar dense_batch_size, (b) a DAG whose node set contains at least {KQV, Attention, O, Up, Gate, Act, Down, AG, AR} and whose edges reflect the standard transformer dependency ordering, and (c) an interference-free (kernel, batch_size)->time lookup keyed by discrete batch sizes.

sub_tasks.requirements: Code has been implemented that instantiates a MILP model (e.g., via PuLP, Pyomo, or gurobipy) with decision variables representing per-nano-operation (batch_size, start_time, end_time, ordering slot) and a boolean placement matrix over the pipeline.

verification.spec: Import the auto-search MILP builder. Construct a model on a small toy input and inspect the returned solver instance. Verify it is a pulp/pyomo/gurobipy Model object. Enumerate variables and confirm presence of per-nano-op batch_size (Integer), start_time (Continuous or Integer), end_time, and a boolean ordering/placement matrix indexed by (nano_op, time_slot).

sub_tasks.requirements: Code has been implemented so that a Stage-I MILP objective explicitly minimizes total pipeline execution time (makespan of the last compute-bound nano-operation), reflecting the goal of removing 'WASTED' compute bubbles.

verification.spec: Import the Stage-I MILP builder and construct the model for a small toy input. Inspect the objective function via the solver API (e.g., model.objective) and assert the sense is minimization and the expression is the makespan (max end_time over compute-bound nano-ops) — verify at least one compute-bound nano-op's end_time variable appears in the objective and no memory- or network-bound-only nano-op end_time appears alone.

sub_tasks.requirements: All MILP constraints described in Section 4.1.2 are implemented.

Code has been implemented so that each parent operation is split into at least two nano-operations at the start of the search, with a per-operation counter n_nano_ops[op] >= 2 enforced in the MILP formulation.

verification.spec: Build the Stage-I MILP for a toy 2-op model. For each parent op, count the number of created nano-ops and assert >=2. Additionally, attempt to construct with n_nano_ops[op]=1 and verify a ValueError/assertion is raised.

sub_tasks.requirements: Code has been implemented that restricts each nano-operation's batch size to the discrete set {128, 256, ..., B_dense} (multiples of 128 up to the dense batch size) via integer constraints in the MILP, and rejects any candidate outside this set in a unit test.

verification.spec: Build the MILP with B_dense=2048. Extract the domain of batch_size decision variables and assert values are in {128, 256, ..., 2048}. Then submit a candidate solution with batch_size=200 (not a multiple of 128) and confirm the model reports infeasible or the validator rejects it.

sub_tasks.requirements: Code has been implemented that sets each nano-operation's execution time from the interference-free (kernel, batch_size) -> time lookup, so that changing the profiled time for a specific (kernel, batch_size) shifts that nano-op's duration in the MILP by the same amount.

verification.spec: Build the MILP with a synthetic profile that maps (KQV, 256) -> 1.0 ms. Solve and record the KQV nano-op's duration. Rebuild with (KQV, 256) -> 5.0 ms. Solve again and assert the KQV nano-op's duration increased by exactly 4.0 ms in the new solution.

sub_tasks.requirements: Code has been implemented that encodes the dependency rule 'two nano-ops are dependent iff their parent ops are dependent AND their input batch ranges intersect'; a unit test with ranges (0-255) and (128-383) reports a dependency while (0-127) and (128-255) reports none.

verification.spec: Call the dependency-detection function with parents=(dep_op_A, dep_op_B) and ranges (0-255) & (128-383); assert dependency=True. Call again with ranges (0-127) & (128-255); assert dependency=False. Call with non-dependent parents and any ranges; assert dependency=False.

sub_tasks.requirements: Code has been implemented that forbids temporal overlap of two nano-operations bounded by the same resource class (compute-compute, memory-memory, or network-network) in the MILP, and a unit test rejects a schedule that places two GEMM nano-ops in the same time slot.

verification.spec: Build the MILP and attempt to inject a candidate schedule with two GEMM (compute) nano-ops occupying overlapping time intervals. Call the constraint-validation routine and assert it returns infeasible/violation. Then submit a schedule where one is compute and one is memory-bound over the same interval, and assert it is accepted.

sub_tasks.requirements: Code has been implemented that enumerates equivalent network-collective transformations (e.g., an AllGather realized as an AllReduce under a different weight-partitioning) as alternative candidate nano-operations with their own timing entries, so that Stage-I can choose the shortest variant.

verification.spec: Import the network-transform enumeration module. Given an AG parent node with a specified weight-partitioning, call the enumerator and assert the returned list contains at least the {original AG, equivalent AR under alternate partition} candidates, each with its own timing entry. Verify that these are added as alternative variables in the MILP.

sub_tasks.requirements: Code has been implemented that enforces per-nano-op batch-partition disjointness within a parent operation (union of nano-batch ranges equals [0, B_dense], intersections are empty) via linear constraints.

verification.spec: Build the MILP with B_dense=2048. Solve. Iterate over each parent op and collect the batch_range of its nano-ops; assert the union covers [0, 2048] and pairwise intersections are empty. Then inject a candidate solution with overlapping ranges and assert the constraint check reports infeasibility.

sub_tasks.requirements: The Stage-I outer search loop and termination criteria are implemented.

Code has been implemented that, after solving the MILP with n_nano_ops = 2 for every op, detects residual compute bubbles in the resulting schedule (contiguous intervals with no compute-bound nano-op scheduled) and identifies which parent operation borders each bubble.

verification.spec: Solve Stage-I with n_nano_ops=2 uniformly on a toy schedule engineered to leave a compute gap. Call the bubble-detection routine on the resulting schedule; assert it returns >=1 (start, end) interval with no compute nano-op scheduled, and reports the adjacent parent op(s) identifiers correctly.

sub_tasks.requirements: Code has been implemented that increments n_nano_ops for the operation(s) adjacent to detected bubbles and re-solves the MILP, iterating this refinement loop until re-solving yields no makespan improvement.

verification.spec: Run the refinement loop on a toy input where n_nano_ops=2 leaves detectable bubbles. Verify that on each iteration n_nano_ops for the identified adjacent op increases by 1, the MILP is re-solved, and that the loop exits when the new makespan >= previous. Assert the returned schedule has smaller makespan than the initial one.

sub_tasks.requirements: Code has been implemented that runs the MILP solver in feasibility-first mode (e.g., MIP gap relaxed, time limit set) rather than searching for a provable optimum, matching the paper's statement that a feasible-not-optimal solution is preferred.

verification.spec: Import the MILP solver-invocation function. Inspect its solver configuration: assert either a positive time_limit is set (finite wall-clock cap) OR the MIP gap is relaxed (>0), i.e., not requesting a proven optimum. Failing test: set time_limit=None and mip_gap=0 and confirm the wrapper rewrites/warns.

sub_tasks.requirements: Code has been implemented that emits, on completion, a structured pipeline record listing every nano-operation with fields {parent_op, batch_range, kernel_id, start_time, end_time, resource_class}, suitable for consumption by Stage II.

verification.spec: Run Stage-I on a toy model and dump the emitted schedule to JSON. Load it and, for each entry, assert presence of keys {parent_op, batch_range, kernel_id, start_time, end_time, resource_class}. sub_tasks.requirements: Chunked-prefill batch formation targeting a fixed dense batch size (2048 for LLaMA-2-70B), asynchronous CPU-side batch formation overlapping with GPU execution, PagedAttention page-table updates, and OOM avoidance via CPU offload are implemented per Section 4.2.1.

Chunked-prefill batch formation composes a fixed-size dense token batch by prioritizing unfinished decode tokens and chunking prefill tokens at token granularity (SarathiServe-style) to fill remaining capacity.

Code has been implemented that exposes a `Scheduler`/`BatchFormer` object accepting a configurable `dense_batch_size` parameter (i.e., total token budget) and holding queues for prefill and decode requests.

verification.spec: Import the runtime package and instantiate the Scheduler/BatchFormer class with a `dense_batch_size` keyword argument. Assert the object exposes attributes/queues for pending prefill requests and pending decode requests (e.g., `prefill_queue`, `decode_queue` or equivalent), and that `dense_batch_size` is stored on the instance.

sub_tasks.requirements: Code has been implemented such that on each iteration the batch formation first appends tokens from unfinished decode requests, then fills the remaining slots with prefill tokens taken from the head of pending prefill requests, chunking a single prefill request across multiple iterations when its length exceeds the remaining budget.

verification.spec: Create a Scheduler with dense_batch_size=2048, enqueue several decode requests summing to fewer than 2048 tokens and a large pending prefill request. Call the batch-formation method and assert (a) all pending decode tokens appear first in the emitted batch, (b) the remainder is filled with a chunk of the head prefill request, and (c) if the prefill request's remaining length exceeds the free slots, only a chunk of it is consumed and the rest stays queued for the next iteration.

sub_tasks.requirements: A unit test constructs a scheduler with `dense_batch_size=2048`, injects a mix of prefill and decode requests, and asserts that the emitted batch always sums to exactly the dense batch size (padding empty slots with prefill chunks) whenever pending prefills are non-empty.

verification.spec: Run the shipped unit test that constructs a scheduler with dense_batch_size=2048, injects mixed prefill+decode requests, and asserts every emitted batch's total token count equals 2048 exactly when pending prefill work is available.

sub_tasks.requirements: A unit test verifies that a request finishing its prefill stage transitions into the decode queue on the next iteration, and that its per-iteration token contribution drops from its prefill chunk size to exactly 1 decode token.

verification.spec: Run the unit test that submits a single request, drives the scheduler through enough iterations to finish its prefill chunk, and asserts the request moves from prefill_queue to decode_queue and its per-iteration token contribution drops from the prefill chunk size to exactly 1.

sub_tasks.requirements: The default dense batch size used for the LLaMA-2-70B end-to-end configuration is 2048 tokens (matching Section 4.2.1's example of 1 prefill request of ~2048 tokens plus ~256 decode tokens combined into the GEMM batch); verified by inspecting the runtime configuration/CLI defaults.

verification.spec: Inspect the runtime configuration file (YAML/JSON) or CLI defaults for the LLaMA-2-70B end-to-end config and assert dense_batch_size (or equivalent token-budget field) is set to 2048.

sub_tasks.requirements: Peak-memory-aware admission control predicts future KV-cache usage per request and offloads to CPU (without recomputation on reload) when the GPU would otherwise OOM.
Code has been implemented that tracks, for every active request, the number of tokens decoded so far and estimates its remaining decode length using the workload's average decode length.

verification.spec: Instantiate the scheduler with a configured average decode length, add several active requests each having decoded a different number of tokens, and call the memory-prediction/tracking API. Assert each request reports (a) its decoded-so-far count matching what was fed, and (b) an estimated remaining decode length computed from the configured average.

sub_tasks.requirements: Code has been implemented that predicts peak future GPU memory usage from (i) current KV-cache footprint, (ii) estimated remaining KV growth of running requests, and (iii) KV needed to admit a candidate new prefill request; and only admits the new prefill when the prediction stays within GPU memory limits.

verification.spec: Configure a scheduler with a small GPU-memory cap. Populate with running requests whose predicted peak KV usage nearly fills memory, then attempt to admit a new prefill request whose KV admission would exceed the cap: assert the scheduler rejects/defers admission. Then reduce running requests so the predicted peak fits and assert the same candidate is admitted.

sub_tasks.requirements: Code has been implemented that, when the GPU actually exhausts memory mid-run, evicts one or more in-flight requests' KV-cache to host CPU memory and later reloads them into GPU pages so that decoding resumes from the offloaded state without any prefill recomputation.

verification.spec: Force an OOM condition mid-run (shrink free-page pool below current requirement). Assert one or more running requests' KV blocks are moved to a CPU-resident offload table with matching token ids and page contents. After freeing pages, call the scheduler again and assert the offloaded request is reloaded into GPU pages and decoding resumes from the offloaded token position (no prefill recomputation call is triggered).

sub_tasks.requirements: A unit test forces the memory predictor into an OOM condition by shrinking the free-page pool, runs one scheduling step, and asserts that (a) the offending request is placed in a CPU-resident offload table with matching token ids, and (b) after freeing pages a subsequent step reloads it into GPU KV pages without invoking the prefill code path.

verification.spec: Run the shipped unit test that shrinks the free-page pool to trigger the OOM path, invokes one scheduling step, asserts the offloaded request appears in a CPU offload table with matching token ids, then frees pages and asserts a subsequent step reloads it into GPU KV pages ready to decode.

sub_tasks.requirements: Asynchronous scheduling overlaps CPU-side batch formation with GPU execution: the batch for iteration i+1 is formed before iteration i completes, at the cost of a one-iteration delay in EOS handling.

Code has been implemented that runs batch formation on a CPU thread/coroutine which enqueues the next iteration's batch (memory estimation, EOS retirement, new-request admission, page-table adjustment) while a separate stream/thread drives the GPU forward pass, using CUDA events (or equivalent) to synchronize handoff.

verification.spec: Instantiate the runtime's async scheduler with a mocked GPU step (records timestamps of calls). Run several iterations and assert that the CPU-side batch formation for iteration i+1 runs concurrently with the GPU step of iteration i (formation start_time_{i+1} < gpu_end_time_i), and that CUDA events or equivalent sync primitives are recorded between them.

sub_tasks.requirements: Code has been implemented such that at iteration i the scheduler launches iteration i+1's batch before iteration i's output tokens are read back, and only detects EOS tokens produced at iteration i during formation of iteration i+2's batch (i.e., a one-iteration EOS-detection delay is present by design).

verification.spec: Using a mocked GPU step that records the iteration index at which each request was fed and returns EOS on request, verify the ordering: iteration i+1's batch is formed and dispatched before iteration i's output tokens are read, and that EOS produced at step i is only detected during the formation call for iteration i+2.

sub_tasks.requirements: A unit test with a mocked GPU step function verifies that consecutive iterations' batch-formation and GPU-execution wall-times overlap (the async-scheduling total wall-time is strictly less than the sum of the two components), confirming CPU/GPU pipelining.

verification.spec: Run the shipped async-scheduling unit test with a mocked GPU step function that sleeps a known duration. Measure total wall time for N iterations under async mode vs. a synchronous baseline and assert async_total_time < formation_time_per_step * N + gpu_time_per_step * N (i.e. overlap occurred).

sub_tasks.requirements: A unit test simulates a request that produces EOS at iteration i and asserts that it is removed from the batch at iteration i+2 (not i+1), reproducing the deliberate one-token overshoot introduced by async scheduling.

verification.spec: Run the shipped unit test that stubs a request to emit EOS at iteration i, and asserts the request remains in the batch at iteration i+1 (one-token overshoot) and is removed only at iteration i+2.

sub_tasks.requirements: On a workload with average decode length >100 (e.g., Splitwise or ShareGPT statistics from Table 4), the per-request overhead of the one-extra-decode-token side-effect of async scheduling is measured to be < 1% of total decode tokens generated, matching the paper's <1% claim in Section 4.2.1.

verification.spec: Run a workload driver against the runtime using Splitwise or ShareGPT input/output length distributions (avg decode length >100 per Table 4). Compute overhead = (extra_decode_tokens_from_async / total_decode_tokens_generated). Assert overhead < 1%.

sub_tasks.requirements: PagedAttention page-table updates are integrated into batch formation so that new prefill/decode tokens acquire GPU pages and retired requests release them each iteration.

Code has been implemented that maintains a PagedAttention block/page table (fixed-size KV blocks with per-request page lists) and a free-page pool, exposed via allocate/free operations used by the scheduler.

verification.spec: Construct the PagedAttention block manager with a fixed page size and total number of pages. Allocate pages for two requests, verify each request has a page list of expected length, verify the free-page pool decreased by that many pages, then free one request and assert its pages are returned to the free pool.

sub_tasks.requirements: Code has been implemented so that during batch formation the scheduler adjusts the page table by (a) allocating pages for newly prefilled tokens and additional decode tokens crossing a page boundary, and (b) freeing pages of retired requests, before the GPU forward pass reads the block table.

verification.spec: Run the scheduler through iterations where (a) a new prefill request is admitted (assert its pages are allocated in the block table before the GPU forward call), (b) a decode request crosses a page boundary (assert an additional page is allocated), and (c) a request retires (assert its pages are freed before the next forward call reads the block table).

sub_tasks.requirements: A unit test asserts that after adding a prefill request of N tokens, the request's page list has ceil(N / page_size) entries drawn from the free pool, and that after the request retires those exact page ids are returned to the free pool.

verification.spec: Run the shipped unit test that adds an N-token prefill request, asserts len(request.page_list) == ceil(N/page_size) and that all page ids are drawn from the free pool, retires the request, and asserts exactly those page ids are returned to the free pool.

sub_tasks.requirements: A unit test verifies that the block table handed to the attention kernel for a batch reflects the page-table updates performed in that iteration's asynchronous formation step (no stale block ids).

verification.spec: Run the shipped unit test that intercepts the block table passed to the attention kernel during iteration i and asserts it reflects the page allocations/frees performed by the async formation step for that same iteration (compare to expected block ids from a synchronous reference).

sub_tasks.requirements: The runtime launches nano-operations for each formed batch respecting auto-search ordering, using CUDA events to enforce cross-stream dependencies (per Section 5).

Code has been implemented such that, given the auto-search-produced nano-operation schedule, the runtime launches the corresponding CUDA kernels for each nano-batch on the appropriate streams and inserts CUDA events to enforce ordering dependencies between them.

verification.spec: Feed the runtime a fixed nano-operation schedule (as produced by auto-search) and verify: (a) each nano-op's launcher is invoked with the corresponding CUDA kernel and stream identifier from the schedule, and (b) CUDA events (cudaEventRecord / cudaStreamWaitEvent, or the runtime's abstraction) are inserted between operations whose schedule declares a dependency.

sub_tasks.requirements: A behavioral test confirms that a nano-operation declared to depend on another (per the schedule) does not begin execution on its stream until the CUDA event recorded by the producer has been signaled (verified via injected timing/callback).

verification.spec: Construct a two-node schedule with an explicit dependency and inject a callback into the producer kernel that records the wall-clock time when the CUDA event is signaled. Assert the consumer nano-operation's start time is >= that recorded signal time (or, using a mock CUDA runtime, assert the consumer's stream-wait call blocks until the producer's event.record call).

sub_tasks.requirements: The runtime implementation totals approximately ~10K lines of CUDA and ~6K lines of Python as reported in Section 5 (verified by counting non-blank, non-comment source lines in the CUDA and Python source directories, within ±30%).

verification.spec: Run `cloc` (or an equivalent SLOC counter) over the runtime source directories, counting only .cu/.cuh/.cpp/.h under the CUDA implementation dir and .py under the Python dir, excluding blank lines and comments. Assert CUDA LOC is within ±30% of 10000 AND Python LOC is within ±30% of 6000.

sub_tasks.requirements: Simultaneous per-layer KV offload after KQV generation, LRU CPU+SSD hierarchical cache, contiguous-then-scatter load path for PagedAttention, and NUMA-aware thread binding are implemented as in Section 4.2.2.

Per-layer simultaneous offloading path: after KQV generation in each transformer layer, the newly produced K/V vectors are copied device-to-host before being appended to the on-GPU KV-cache, scheduled to overlap with FFN compute so that host and GPU hold identical KV copies for on-the-fly requests.

Code has been implemented that installs a per-layer offload hook triggered immediately after the KQV-generation nano-operations of each decoder layer, before the KV vectors are scattered into the paged KV-cache.

verification.spec: Instrument the decoder-layer forward path to record hook invocations. Run one iteration and assert that for every layer the offload hook fires immediately after the KQV nano-ops complete and before the paged-scatter kernel writes K/V into the paged KV cache.

sub_tasks.requirements: Code has been implemented so that the K and V tensors read at the offload site are contiguous in GPU memory (i.e. the raw KQV-generation output, not the already-scattered paged layout), enabling a single cudaMemcpyAsync per layer.

verification.spec: At the offload site, capture the K and V tensor pointers/strides and assert they refer to a contiguous GPU buffer (K.is_contiguous() and V.is_contiguous() are True and stride matches shape), i.e., the raw KQV output prior to paged scatter, and that the offload uses a single cudaMemcpyAsync per layer (count copy calls == num_layers per iteration).

sub_tasks.requirements: Code has been implemented that submits the KV device-to-host copy on a stream/event ordering that overlaps it with the compute-bound FFN (Up/Gate/Down) nano-operations of the same layer, rather than on the default stream that would serialize with attention.

verification.spec: Record CUDA stream/event annotations (or use Nsight/CUPTI events in a small profiling harness) around one decoder layer and assert the D2H KV copy is queued on a non-default stream ordered to overlap with the Up/Gate/Down FFN nano-ops of the same layer (copy start_time >= UGD start_time and copy end_time <= UGD end_time, or the copy stream != attention stream).

sub_tasks.requirements: A behavioral test verifies that under a fixed dense batch size the number of bytes offloaded per iteration is (approximately) constant across iterations, matching the paper's claim that offload volume is balanced by design.

verification.spec: Run the runtime for N iterations at a fixed dense_batch_size with KV offloading enabled and record bytes offloaded per iteration. Assert the coefficient of variation (std/mean) of the per-iteration offload volume is small (e.g., < 5%), matching the paper's 'balanced by design' claim.

sub_tasks.requirements: Hierarchical CPU+SSD KV-cache with LRU eviction: the host tier holds a bounded pool of past-round KV blocks and evicts to SSD when full; incoming next-round requests retrieve their KV from CPU when present, otherwise from SSD.

Code has been implemented that defines a CPU-tier KV-block store with a configurable byte capacity and an LRU ordering data structure (e.g. doubly linked list + hash map) that tracks per-request KV entries by recency of use.

verification.spec: Import the CPU KV-block store module and instantiate it with a byte capacity parameter. Assert it exposes methods to insert/lookup/evict per-request KV entries, and that the internal ordering structure is a doubly-linked-list + hashmap (or equivalent O(1) LRU structure) by checking the class attributes/types or by verifying LRU move-to-front operations complete in O(1) via micro-timing on N=10,100,1000 entries.

sub_tasks.requirements: Code has been implemented that defines an SSD-tier KV-block store which serializes KV blocks to disk (one file/region per request or per block), used as the spill destination when CPU memory is full.

verification.spec: Instantiate the SSD-tier KV-block store with a tmp directory. Write a KV block for a synthetic request id, then read it back and assert byte-equality. Assert that a file/region exists on disk under the tmp path after write, and that the file size matches the KV payload size.

sub_tasks.requirements: Code has been implemented so that when a CPU insertion would exceed the CPU capacity, the LRU-eldest entries are demoted to the SSD tier before the new entry is admitted (no silent drop).

verification.spec: Configure the two-tier cache with a small CPU capacity that fits exactly 3 KV blocks. Insert 3 blocks (A,B,C), then insert a 4th (D). Assert that A (LRU-eldest) has been demoted to the SSD tier (readable from SSD store) and NOT silently dropped, and that D is now present in CPU tier.

sub_tasks.requirements: Code has been implemented for the retrieval path: when a new-round conversation request arrives, the runtime looks up its KV first in the CPU tier and, on miss, in the SSD tier, initiating a load without recomputing prior tokens.

verification.spec: Seed CPU tier with request X's KV; call the retrieval API and assert it returns from CPU (record tier-hit). Then evict X to SSD (fill CPU beyond capacity), call retrieval again and assert it returns from SSD without invoking any prefill/recompute path (mock/spy on the recompute function and assert it was not called).

sub_tasks.requirements: A behavioral unit test seeds the two-tier cache with a known access pattern and asserts that the eviction order matches strict LRU semantics across the CPU→SSD boundary (least-recently-used entry is the first to be demoted).

verification.spec: Run pytest on the unit test file that exercises the two-tier cache: insert entries [A,B,C,D] with CPU capacity 3, touch B (access), then insert E. Assert eviction order is A first (LRU), then C (next LRU after B was touched). Verify the SSD tier contains {A,C} in that insertion order and CPU tier contains {B,D,E}.

sub_tasks.requirements: Contiguous-then-scatter host-to-device load path: rather than copying host KV directly into the fragmented PagedAttention page slots, NanoFlow first stages the data into a contiguous GPU buffer with one large H2D transfer, then dispatches an on-device scatter kernel to place pages at their final fragmented destinations.
Code has been implemented that allocates a contiguous GPU staging buffer sized to hold the KV blocks being loaded for the incoming request batch (reused across loads to avoid per-load cudaMalloc).

verification.spec: Import the KV-loader module and verify it exposes a staging-buffer allocator that (a) accepts a byte-size argument sized to a KV batch, (b) allocates via torch.cuda or cudaMalloc exactly once at init, and (c) returns the same device pointer on repeated calls (reuse). Assert allocation count == 1 after N=10 load requests by patching cudaMalloc/torch.cuda.caching_allocator.

sub_tasks.requirements: Code has been implemented that issues a single contiguous cudaMemcpyAsync (HostToDevice) from the pinned host KV region into the staging buffer, rather than one memcpy per PagedAttention page.

verification.spec: Instrument the loader by wrapping cudaMemcpyAsync (or torch equivalent) with a counter. Load a KV region for a request with K pages. Assert exactly ONE HostToDevice memcpy call was issued (not K), and the byte count equals total_pages * page_bytes.

sub_tasks.requirements: Code has been implemented that launches a device-side scatter kernel taking (staging_ptr, page_table, num_pages) and writes each page slice into the fragmented physical page indexed by PagedAttention's page table.

verification.spec: Import the scatter kernel launcher. Build a synthetic staging tensor with distinct per-page byte patterns and a random page_table permuting them to fragmented destination indices. Launch the scatter kernel and assert that each destination page (by page_table index) contains the corresponding source page bytes.

sub_tasks.requirements: A behavioral test verifies functional equivalence: KV blocks loaded via the contiguous-then-scatter path produce byte-identical final page contents to a reference direct-scatter H2D copy for the same page_table.

verification.spec: Build a KV payload of known bytes on host. Load it into GPU pages via two paths: (1) contiguous H2D then scatter kernel, (2) reference direct per-page cudaMemcpy to fragmented destinations. Read both back and assert torch.equal on every physical page. Test with page_table permutations of length 32 and 256.

sub_tasks.requirements: A microbenchmark measures effective H2D bandwidth of the contiguous-then-scatter load path versus a direct fragmented-destination copy for the same total KV payload; the contiguous-then-scatter path achieves 7-10x higher host-to-device bandwidth as reported in Section 4.2.2.

verification.spec: Run a microbenchmark that copies a fixed KV payload (e.g. 4GB total) from pinned host memory to fragmented GPU PagedAttention destinations two ways: (a) direct per-page cudaMemcpyAsync, (b) contiguous H2D into staging + device scatter kernel. Time each with cuda.Event and compute effective GB/s. Report the ratio bandwidth_b / bandwidth_a.

sub_tasks.requirements: NUMA-aware thread binding for the KV offload/load path so that host-side copy worker threads execute on the NUMA node local to the pinned KV buffer, reducing cross-socket memory traffic.
Code has been implemented that queries the NUMA topology (e.g. via libnuma or /sys/devices/system/node) at startup and records, per GPU, the NUMA node closest to that GPU.

verification.spec: Import the NUMA-topology detection module and call its init/query function. Assert it returns a per-GPU dict mapping gpu_id -> numa_node_id, and cross-check against `nvidia-smi topo -m` output or /sys/class/drm/card*/device/numa_node for at least GPU 0.

sub_tasks.requirements: Code has been implemented that allocates the pinned host KV region on the NUMA node local to the target GPU and pins the offload/load worker threads' CPU affinity to that node (numa_bind / pthread_setaffinity_np).

verification.spec: Initialize the offload subsystem for GPU 0. Read /proc/self/numa_maps (or use libnuma get_mempolicy) on the pinned KV buffer address and assert its bind node == the NUMA node returned for GPU 0. Read the worker thread's affinity mask via sched_getaffinity and assert it is a subset of the cpus on that NUMA node.

sub_tasks.requirements: A behavioral test spawns the offload worker(s) and asserts that their CPU affinity mask and the page-residency of the pinned KV region both lie on the same NUMA node as the associated GPU.

verification.spec: Run pytest that spawns the offload worker threads, then for each worker calls sched_getaffinity and move_pages()/get_mempolicy() on the pinned KV region address. Assert both are on the same NUMA node as the GPU device (as reported by the topology query).

sub_tasks.requirements: End-to-end effect of the hierarchical offloading subsystem on pipeline execution.

An end-to-end measurement compares NanoFlow with KV offloading disabled vs enabled on the LLaMA-2-70B pipeline and reports the per-GPU throughput slowdown attributable to offload-induced kernel interference; the slowdown is approximately 3.0% as reported in the ablation study of Section 6.4.

verification.spec: Run the NanoFlow LLaMA-2-70B pipeline on a fixed workload twice: (a) KV offloading disabled, (b) KV offloading enabled. Measure per-GPU tokens/s over a 5-minute steady-state window each. Compute slowdown = (a - b) / a * 100.

sub_tasks.requirements: A multi-round replay driven by the LMSYS-Chat workload measures the total compute (in TFLOPs or equivalently prefill-token count) executed with hierarchical KV offloading enabled versus a recomputation baseline that has no offloading; enabling offloading reduces compute by approximately 3.02x as claimed in Section 6.4.

verification.spec: Replay the LMSYS-Chat multi-round workload twice on NanoFlow LLaMA-2-70B: (a) hierarchical KV offload enabled (subsequent rounds reload cached KV), (b) offload disabled, so subsequent rounds recompute prefill. Count total prefill tokens processed (or total TFLOPs) end-to-end. Report ratio compute_b / compute_a.

sub_tasks.requirements: A behavioral smoke test loads LLaMA-2-70B in FP16 with tensor parallelism = 8 under vLLM and successfully completes generation for at least one prompt, confirming the installed vLLM baseline is runnable end-to-end.

sub_tasks.requirements: Code has been implemented to launch DeepSpeed-FastGen (MII persistent pipeline) with the max-ragged-batch-size flag exposed as a configurable parameter that is swept to select the highest-throughput setting per workload.

sub_tasks.requirements: A behavioral smoke test starts a DeepSpeed-FastGen server for LLaMA-2-70B (TP=8, FP16) and returns valid decoded tokens for a sample prompt, confirming the installed baseline is runnable end-to-end.

verification.spec: Start a DeepSpeed-FastGen (MII) persistent pipeline for LLaMA-2-70B in FP16 with tensor_parallel=8. Submit prompt 'Hello, world.' with max_new_tokens=16 and assert the response contains a non-empty decoded string and no exception is raised.

sub_tasks.requirements: TensorRT-LLM baseline is installed at the exact pinned version and its engine is compiled with the paged KV-cache, dynamic batching, and max-num-tokens settings described in Section 6.1.
Code has been implemented to install TensorRT-LLM at version v0.8.0 (commit ID 5955b8a) from https://github.com/NVIDIA/TensorRT-LLM, pinned via a build script or requirements file.

verification.spec: Run the pinned install script for TensorRT-LLM. Then `python -c 'import tensorrt_llm; print(tensorrt_llm.__version__)'` and assert it starts with '0.8.0'. Additionally verify the installed source or wheel metadata pins commit '5955b8a' (grep pip freeze or the git submodule/URL used in install).

sub_tasks.requirements: Code has been implemented to compile a TensorRT-LLM engine for LLaMA-2-70B (FP16, TP=8) with paged KV-cache enabled and dynamic (in-flight) batching enabled at build time.

verification.spec: Run the TensorRT-LLM engine build script for LLaMA-2-70B with dtype=float16, tp_size=8, --paged_kv_cache=enable, --use_inflight_batching=enable (or the equivalent v0.8.0 flags). sub_tasks.requirements: Code has been implemented to compute max-num-tokens for TensorRT-LLM by determining the maximum KV-cache capacity that fits in GPU memory for the loaded model (as described in Section 6.1), and to pass this value to the engine build/runtime.

verification.spec: Call the helper that computes max_num_tokens: it should query total GPU memory, subtract model weight bytes (2 * PModel for FP16) and activation overhead, and return the token capacity that saturates remaining memory for KV-cache. Assert the returned value is positive, larger than 2048, and that it is actually threaded into the engine build/runtime args (grep the build config).

sub_tasks.requirements: A behavioral smoke test loads the compiled TensorRT-LLM engine and generates output for at least one prompt of LLaMA-2-70B FP16 on 8xA100, confirming the installed baseline is runnable end-to-end.

sub_tasks.requirements: A common request-issuing harness drives all three baselines (and NanoFlow) with identical workloads so throughput and latency comparisons are apples-to-apples.

Code has been implemented for a single harness module that issues requests to each of the three baseline servers (vLLM, DeepSpeed-FastGen, TensorRT-LLM) and to NanoFlow through a uniform backend interface.

verification.spec: Import the harness module and instantiate a uniform backend interface for each of {nanoflow, vllm, deepspeed_fastgen, tensorrt_llm}; assert each exposes a common `submit(requests)` / `run(workload)` API and dispatches to the appropriate underlying server.

sub_tasks.requirements: The harness supports both offline throughput mode (issue full sampled workload as fast as possible) and online latency mode (Poisson/exponential inter-arrival at a configurable request rate), matching the offline and normalized-latency experimental protocols.

verification.spec: Run the harness in both `--mode offline` and `--mode online --request-rate 4` against a mock backend; assert offline submits all requests concurrently while online produces exponential inter-arrival times matching a Poisson process (KS test p>0.05).

sub_tasks.requirements: The harness reads (input_len, output_len) pairs sampled from the datasets (Splitwise / LMSYS-Chat-1M / ShareGPT) and constant-length settings, and injects the sampled output length as max_tokens on every backend so all systems generate the same number of tokens per request.

verification.spec: Invoke the harness with each of the six workloads (const_512_512, const_1024_512, const_512_1024, splitwise, lmsys_chat, sharegpt) against a mock backend that records the max_tokens argument on every request; assert max_tokens equals the sampled output_len for every request across all backends.

sub_tasks.requirements: The harness records per-request completion timestamps and generated token counts to a shared log format, and computes per-GPU total throughput (tokens/s/GPU) and normalized latency (ms/token) with the exact formulas used in Sections 6.2 and 6.3.
